title: parseInt(null, 36) returns 1112745
assumption: Passing null where a string is expected is harmless, or at worst gives you 0 or NaN.

input.description: A missing or unset form field, config value, or optional function argument that falls through to `parseInt` without a guard, combined with a non-default radix such as base36 (used for compact id encoding).

what_goes_wrong: A missing value that should produce 0, NaN, or an error instead silently produces a real-looking, nonzero integer -- 1112745 -- which can pass a `typeof x === 'number' && !isNaN(x)` guard and flow deep into the system before anyone notices the input was never actually a number.
why: `parseInt`'s first argument is coerced to a string before parsing, and `String(null)` is the literal string `"null"`. In base 36, digits run 0-9 then a-z representing 10-35, so every character of "null" (n, u, l, l) is a valid base-36 digit, and the whole string parses successfully as a number -- specifically 1112745. Nothing about this path raises an error or returns NaN, because from `parseInt`'s point of view it was simply handed a valid base-36 numeral.

repros.expected_output: TypeError: int() can't convert non-string with explicit base

fix: Guard against `null`/`undefined` before calling `parseInt` rather than relying on it to fail loudly; it won't, for any radix where the stringified sentinel's letters happen to be valid digits.

sources.title: ECMA-262: parseInt (string coercion of the first argument)

test_cases.note: A function wrapping parseInt with a non-10 radix should explicitly reject null/undefined rather than let String() coercion through.
